If the speed of a satellite that is in a circular orbit is lowered, the satellite will no longer stay in that circular orbit.  It will fall into an **elliptical orbit** whose symmetric point (at the new perigee) is at the same altitude as the original orbit.  The new ellipse has a **smaller semi‑major axis** than the old one, and therefore the orbital period shortens.

---

### 1.  Why the radius changes

For a circular orbit the required centripetal acceleration is  

\[
\frac{v_{\rm circ}^{2}}{r}=\frac{GM_{\oplus}}{r^{2}}
\]

so the speed that must be maintained at radius \(r\) is  

\[
v_{\rm circ}=\sqrt{\frac{GM_{\oplus}}{r}}\quad\text{(1)}
\]

If the satellite’s speed is **decreased** to any \(v< v_{\rm circ}\), the required
centripetal acceleration is \(v^{2}/r\), which is **less** than the gravitational
acceleration \(GM_{\oplus}/r^{2}\).  Consequently, the satellite accelerates
inward and its orbit is no longer circular.  The satellite is now on an
elliptical orbit with the present radius \(r\) being its **apogee** (the
slowest point).  Using the vis‑viva equation,
\[
v^{2}=GM_{\oplus}\!\left(\frac{2}{r}-\frac{1}{a}\right)\qquad\text{(2)}
\]
and solving for the semi‑major axis \(a\), we find

\[
\frac{1}{a}= \frac{2}{r}-\frac{v^{2}}{GM_{\oplus}}
            \approx\frac{2}{r}-\frac{v_{\rm circ}^{2}}{GM_{\oplus}}
            =\frac{2}{r}-\frac{1}{r}\;=\;\frac{1}{r}
\]

for a *circular* orbit.  Because the actual speed is smaller, \(v^{2}\) is
less than \(v_{\rm circ}^{2}\) and the right‑hand side is larger:

\[
\frac{1}{a}= \frac{2}{r}-\frac{v^{2}}{GM_{\oplus}}
            =\frac{1}{r}+\frac{|\,\Delta v^{2}\,|}{GM_{\oplus}}\;>\;\frac{1}{r}
\]

Hence \(a<r\).  The semi‑major axis of the new orbit is therefore
smaller than the old radius, i.e. the satellite’s orbit moves closer to the
Earth.  The new orbit will have a perigee that lies at the same altitude
where the speed was reduced, while the apogee is the previous radius
(and will be the next lowest altitude the satellite will reach).

---

### 2.  Why the period changes

Kepler’s third law for any orbit (circular or elliptical) is

\[
T = 2\pi\,\sqrt{\frac{a^{3}}{GM_{\oplus}}}\quad\text{(3)}
\]

where \(a\) is the semi‑major axis.  Since \(a\) has become **smaller** after
the speed reduction, the cube of the semi‑major axis shrinks:

\[
a_{\rm new} < a_{\rm old}=r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{a_{\rm new}^{3}}{a_{\rm old}^{3}} < 1.
\]

Thus

\[
T_{\rm new} = 2\pi\,\sqrt{\frac{a_{\rm new}^{3}}{GM_{\oplus}}}
   < 2\pi\,\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM_{\oplus}}}
   = T_{\rm old},
\]

so the orbital period is **shorter** than before.  The satellite
revolves faster in the smaller orbit.

---

### 3.  Summary

| Quantity | Initial state | After a speed‑decrease | Reason |
|----------|---------------|------------------------|--------|
| Radial distance | Fixed \(r\) (circular) | New orbit with \(a < r\) (ellipse) | Conservation of energy & momentum → excess radial acceleration → inward fall |
| Period | \(T_{\rm circ}=2\pi\sqrt{r^{3}/GM_{\oplus}}\) | \(T_{\rm new}=2\pi\sqrt{a^{3}/GM_{\oplus}}\) (shorter) | \(a\) is smaller → Kepler’s third law |

Thus, a satellite whose speed is made smaller will go into a smaller, longer‑time ellipse (but the period is shorter because the semi‑major axis is smaller).  It will continue to undergo this new orbit until another change of speed or any other perturbation (e.g. atmospheric drag) alters the orbit again.
